summary: Defines a YANG data model for configuring and managing the Routing in Fat Trees protocol. It is based on YANG 1.1 and follows the Network Management Datastore Architecture.

eli5.summary: This is a standard settings sheet that lets software configure RIFT on different switches.

subtitle: A YANG data model for configuring RIFT and reading its state, neighbors, database and statistics.

tldr.problem: The Routing in Fat Trees (RIFT) protocol needs a standard, machine-readable way to be configured and monitored on routers from different vendors.
tldr.mechanism: The ietf-rift YANG 1.1 module augments the ietf-routing model so RIFT appears as a control-plane protocol. It groups base protocol and interface configuration with neighbor status, TIE database and statistics, and adds actions and an error notification.
tldr.outcome: Operators and tools can manage RIFT through standard NMDA-compatible interfaces. Vendors are expected to extend the module for vendor-specific parameters. The RFC is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 9719 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2025, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the YANG companion to the RIFT protocol specification in RFC 9692.

sections.title: What the Model Is For
sections.content:
RFC 9692 defines the RIFT (Routing in Fat Trees) protocol. This document defines one YANG 1.1 data model, the module ietf-rift, for managing it. The model is compatible with the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA) of RFC 8342 and imports and augments the ietf-routing model of RFC 8349.

The RFC copies the protocol vocabulary from RFC 9692 for convenience. A Clos or Fat Tree is a folded spine-and-leaf topology with possibly several Points of Delivery (PoDs) and one or more Top of Fabric (ToF) planes. LIEs (Link Information Elements) are exchanged on links to form ThreeWay adjacencies and to carry Zero Touch Provisioning information for levels. TIEs (Topology Information Elements) describe parts of the network such as links and prefixes, and each has a direction (North or South) and a type.

Tree diagrams follow the notation of RFC 8340, and data node names appear without a prefix when the module is clear from context.
sections.eli5: RIFT is a way for the computers that run a big building-sized network to tell each other who is connected to whom. This RFC makes the standard form you fill in to control it.

sections.title: Scope and Structure of the Model
sections.content:
The model configures and manages RIFT and lets a client retrieve operational state and statistics. A user can subscribe to changes in its data nodes using the mechanisms of RFC 8639 and RFC 8641. It holds the basic parameters needed to run the protocol. Occasionally implemented parameters are modelled as optional features, since a system may not allow some advanced parameters to be configured. The model can be extended, and the module description expects vendors to add vendor-specific parameters and policies.

The module augments /routing/control-plane-protocols/control-plane-protocol and declares a list called rift. Each protocol instance has a unique name, so multiple instances are supported. Operational state is combined with the configuration data in the same hierarchy, as NMDA recommends.

Four features can be switched on or off: nonce-delta-adjust (weak nonce delta adjusting used in security), label-switching (label switching for instance distinguishing), tie-security (security for TIE exchange) and link-security (security of the link).
sections.eli5: The sheet has some boxes everyone must fill in and some extra boxes that only some machines have. The extra boxes are marked as options.

sections.title: Organization of the Data
sections.content:
At a high level the model has five elements:

  • Base protocol configuration: settings that affect RIFT operation as a whole (the global container).
  • Interface configuration: settings that affect the interfaces.
  • Neighbor status: information about neighbors.
  • Database: information about TIEs.
  • Statistics: statistics for SPF, interfaces and neighbors.

Under each rift instance the tree has global, a list of interfaces (each with a nested list of neighbors), statistics and database. The database holds a list of TIEs keyed by direction, originator, type and number. A TIE entry can hold node information, prefixes with their metrics and tags, or key-value data.

The RFC also defines a few types: a system-id string made of four groups of four hex digits separated by dots (for example 0021.2FFF.FEB5.6E10), and a level from 0 to 24 where level 0 means a leaf and the top level is the ToF.
sections.eli5: The sheet has parts: the machine's own settings, settings for each plug, a list of neighbors, a big address book of the network, and score counters.

sections.title: Configuration Parameters
sections.content:
Configuration covers node-wide settings and per-interface settings. Features that enhance the protocol, such as BFD (RFC 5881) with flooding reduction, are included.

Examples of node-wide settings in global include system-id, fabric-id, pod, the optional configured-level, an overload container with either an on-startup or an immediate timeout, the node capabilities (hierarchy-indications and flood-reduction), LIE multicast addresses and port, the global link capabilities (BFD, IPv4 forwarding, MTU), and the TIDE generation interval. Security can be set for TIE exchange by a key chain (RFC 8177) or by an explicit key and crypto algorithm. The maximum-nonce-delta leaf, available under the nonce-delta-adjust feature, ranges from 1 to 5 and sets how far a received nonce may be out of range before the packet MUST be discarded.

Per-interface settings include the cost, the flood receive port, a hold time, the address families, the advertised source addresses, whether the link is broadcast capable, whether horizontal links are allowed, link security and link capabilities.
sections.eli5: Settings include the machine's name tag, how important it is, and how it should lock its conversations with a secret key. Each plug on the machine also gets its own small set of settings.

sections.title: State Data and Actions
sections.content:
State data covers the node, interfaces, neighbors and the database. Read-only parts include the node level actually in use, protocol major and minor version, the HAL value and system IDs, miscabled links, each interface's state, and per-neighbor details such as level, sent and received offers, link IDs, cost, bandwidth, BFD state and nonces.

Statistics cover totals of routes, SPF runs, per-interface counters (neighbors up and down, flaps, LIEs sent, received and dropped) and per-neighbor TIE counters (TIEs, TIDEs and TIREs sent, received and retransmitted, and TIEs dropped).

Five YANG actions are defined: clear one neighbor on an interface, clear all neighbors on an interface, clear SPF statistics, clear interface statistics and clear neighbor statistics.
sections.eli5: You can also read the machine's report card, which shows its friends, its address book and counters. A few buttons let you reset a friendship or wipe a counter.

sections.title: Error Notifications
sections.content: The model defines one notification, error-set, so unexpected TIE-level and neighbor-level errors can be reported. It has two parts. tie-level-error lists, per RIFT instance, the TIEs involved by direction, originator, type, number, sequence number, size and lifetimes. neighbor-error lists, per instance and interface, the neighbors involved with their system ID and level.
sections.eli5: When something unexpected happens, the machine can ring a bell and say which message or which neighbor caused the trouble.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module is designed to be accessed through NETCONF (RFC 6241) or RESTCONF (RFC 8040), over SSH or TLS, with RFC 8341 access control available to restrict users to a subset of operations and content.

Writable data nodes may be sensitive. Changing the configuration may force RIFT neighborships to be rebuilt: for example, changing configured-level or system-id rebuilds all neighbor connections of the node, and a wrong change to authentication will break connections permanently, except for already broken ones. Some readable data is sensitive too. The database exposes the detailed topology of the network, which operators may consider confidential. Authentication key data MUST be kept secret, because a compromise would let an attacker forge RIFT packets that are accepted as authentic, potentially compromising the entire domain. The five clear actions can cause neighbor connections to be rebuilt or statistics to be cleared, so access to them should be controlled.
sections.eli5: Anyone who can change these settings can disconnect parts of the network, and anyone who can read them can see the map. So only trusted people should get the keys to the control room.
